name: Mixed air temperature
seoTitle: Mixed air temperature Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Mixed air temperature: work out comp. P₁ from the temp. T₂ and the comp. P₂. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Mixed air temperature calculator turns the temp. T₂, the comp. P₂, the mixed air temperature and the temperature of outside air into comp. P₁. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Mixed air temperature calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mixed air temperature calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports comp. P₁ in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the temp. T₂, the comp. P₂, the mixed air temperature (T) and the temperature of outside air (Tₒₐ).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mixed air temperature calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Comp. P₁=1 − comp. P₂
Temp. T₁=(mixed air temperature (T) − comp. P₂ × temp. T₂) ÷ comp. P₁
Mixed air temperature (Tₛ)=(flow rate of outside air cfmₒₐ × temperature of outside air (Tₒₐ) + flow rate of return air cfmrₐ × temperature of return air (Trₐ)) ÷ (flow rate of outside air cfmₒₐ + flow rate of return air cfmrₐ)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Comp. P₂ = 10 %. The calculator returns Comp. P₁ = 90 %.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Comp. P₁ = 90 % should be roughly the size you expected from Comp. P₂ = 10 %.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • %, opening in percent
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • %, opening in percent
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Flow rate, opening in liters per minute

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mixed air temperature calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the temp. T₂, the comp. P₂ and the mixed air temperature — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Mixed air temperature calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns comp. P₁, derived from the temp. T₂, the comp. P₂ and the mixed air temperature. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mixed air temperature calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the temp. T₂, the comp. P₂, the mixed air temperature and the temperature of outside air, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temp. T₁ in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temp. T₁ opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Comp. P₁ = 90 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Mixed air temperature calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
